passage:
Vandana, you say you will never forgive the friend who told your secret. Let me tell you mine. I'm Harsha. At sixteen my best friend Naveen told the whole class my father had lost his job. For five years I replayed it. I told myself forgiving would mean it hadn't mattered, and it had mattered.
In my twenties my aunt said, "You're carrying his mistake in your bag, and he isn't even here." I realised forgiving didn't mean being friends again or saying it was fine. It meant I could put the weight down. I did, for me. I never went back to that friendship. Naveen wrote once, and I didn't reply, and that was fine.
But my shoulders felt different after.

qa.q: What did Naveen tell the class?
qa.a: Naveen told the whole class that Harsha's father had lost his job.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling during the five years of replaying it?
qa.a: Harsha felt angry and hurt, holding the grudge because forgiving seemed to mean the harm hadn't mattered.

qa.q: What choice inside the story eased the weight without reopening the friendship?
qa.a: Harsha chose to put the weight down for Harsha's own sake, without going back to the friendship or saying it was fine.

qa.q: What did the aunt see when she said Harsha was carrying Naveen's mistake in a bag?
qa.a: The aunt saw that the grudge was costing Harsha while Naveen was not even there to feel it. She named it in a picture, not a lecture.

grounding: An elder recalls holding a grudge because forgiving seemed to mean the harm did not matter; letting go was a release without reconciliation.

passage:
The science-fair project was due at nine the next morning, and Rashmi's only partner was Chinmay, the boy who had told the class about her diary last term. Every time he spoke on the group call she felt the old heat rise in her face. Forgiving him would mean it hadn't mattered, she thought, and it had mattered a lot. The wifi kept dropping.
At eleven at night he sent, "I'm sorry about the diary. I know it was a rotten thing."
She stared at it. Then she wrote, "It was. I'm not ready to be friends. Send me slide four."
"Okay," he wrote.
She felt strange: still angry, but the grip had loosened by one finger. They finished at midnight.

qa.q: What was due at nine the next morning?
qa.a: The science-fair project was due at nine.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling whenever Chinmay spoke on the call?
qa.a: Rashmi felt hot with old anger and hurt, since forgiving him seemed to mean the harm had not mattered.

qa.q: What choice did Rashmi make at eleven that let the project move forward?
qa.a: Rashmi answered that it was a rotten thing, said she was not ready to be friends and asked for slide four. She worked with him without pretending it was fine.

qa.q: What might Chinmay have been feeling when he sent the apology?
qa.a: Chinmay was probably guilty and nervous, hoping for a reply. Sending the apology so late suggests he had been working up to it.

grounding: A teenager replays an old betrayal and refuses to forgive, feeling forgiveness would mean the harm did not matter; letting go does not require friendship.
